definition: A chemical added to separate oil from water. Without it, the fluid might look like mayonnaise.
A large vessel used as the first step of separation to remove the bulk of the water that separates easily from oil.
A small compressor that sucks low-pressure gas off the top of tanks (instead of flaring it) to sell it.
A curve representing the reservoir's ability to deliver fluid to the wellbore at a given bottom-hole pressure.
A truck with a massive reel of continuous steel pipe. It runs pipe into the well while it's still under pressure to clean or stimulate it.
A chemical that coats the steel inside the well to prevent rust and pitting caused by salt water and acid gases.
The standard unit for measuring chemical concentration. (e.g., "We need 500 ppm of inhibitor").
A pressurized trap on a pipeline used to insert or remove a "pig" (cleaning tool) without stopping flow.
Solid chemical pills that release their payload slowly over time or only when crushed downhole.
When sand from the reservoir enters the wellbore and buries the pump or fills the bottom of the casing.
The ratio of how much fluid the pump actually moved vs. how much it should have moved based on its size and speed.
Drilling a well at an angle or curve to hit a specific target (not just straight down).
The calculated amount of oil/gas assigned to a specific well based on the total sales at the battery, rather than what the well meter read (difference due to shrinkage/errors).
Drilling a well at an angle or curve to hit a specific target (not just straight down).
The classic "nodding donkey." A surface motor moves a steel beam up and down, which pulls a rod string and a downhole pump to lift oil.
Injecting a tiny amount of chemical every second of the day to maintain a constant protective film.
The total length of the wellbore (including all curves/turns).
An electrical system used to prevent rust on pipelines and steel tanks by applying a small electrical current.
Ensuring that for every barrel of fluid removed from the reservoir, a barrel of water/gas is injected to maintain pressure.
The total length of the wellbore (including all curves/turns).
A vessel that separates the flow into two streams: Gas and Liquid (oil+water mixed).
A vessel that separates the flow into three streams: Gas, Oil, and Water.
A cable with electrical conductors used to lower logging tools or perforating guns.
A surfactant stick dropped into gas wells. It turns water into light foam so the weak gas pressure can lift it out.
The loss of pressure as fluid moves through pipe, fittings, or restrictors. Facilities engineers size pipe to minimize this.
A device used to measure the load on the pumpjack rod string. The data creates a "dyno card" to diagnose downhole pump problems.
Assembling or disassembling the drilling rig.
The engineering code that governs the design and safety of pressurized vessels (separators, heater treaters). Essential for compliance.
The minimum gas speed required in the tubing to lift liquids (water/oil) to the surface without them falling back down (loading up).
Cycling a well on and off (e.g., Plunger Lift or Timer) to build pressure, rather than flowing continuously.
The shock felt/heard in a pumpjack when the pump is not filling completely (hitting fluid on the downstroke). Causes rod failure.
Assembling or disassembling the drilling rig.
A vessel that removes water vapor from natural gas, usually using glycol (which absorbs water like a sponge).
Small, deep holes eaten into the steel pipe by rust. "Pitting" is dangerous because it causes leaks even if the rest of the pipe looks good.
How often a specific well fails (e.g., "0.5 failures per year").
The network of pipes that collects oil/gas from many wells to a central point.
When drilling mud flows into cracks in the rock instead of returning to the surface.
Basic Sediment & Water. The specific test a pumper performs (using a centrifuge) to determine how much "bad" fluid is in the oil tank before selling.
A small metal strip inserted into a pipe to measure how fast the metal is rusting inside the system.
A graphical plot of the load on the pumpjack rod string. The shape of the "card" tells the engineer if the pump is full, gas-locked, or hitting bottom.
A chemical injected into the flowline to help separate oil from water in the heater treater.
How effectively water or gas injected into the reservoir pushes the oil toward the producing wells.
The network of pipes that collects oil/gas from many wells to a central point.
When drilling mud flows into cracks in the rock instead of returning to the surface.
A chemical (often Hot Oil or Xylene) used to dissolve wax buildup that clogs pipes.
The buildup of hard mineral crust (like kidney stones) inside pipes or pumps, choking off flow.
A well that turns 90 degrees and runs sideways through the oil-bearing rock.
Dumping a large volume of chemicals (corrosion inhibitor or biocide) down the well all at once, rather than dripping it continuously.
Technology used to help get oil to the surface when the reservoir pressure isn't strong enough naturally.
A well that turns 90 degrees and runs sideways through the oil-bearing rock.
When the casing heats up during production and expands, causing the wellhead to physically rise up a few inches.
Dumping a large amount of chemical down the well all at once (e.g., once a week). "Shocking" the system.
A chemical that prevents minerals (calcium/barium) from forming hard rock crusts inside the pipe.
Metal snapping because it was bent back and forth too many times (like a paperclip breaking). Common in rod pumps.

Exploration and Production. Another name for the Upstream sector.
Equivalent Circulating Density. The effective density of drilling fluid when it is moving (pumping).
Enhanced Oil Recovery. Advanced methods (steam, CO2 injection) to get the last bit of oil out.
Electric Submersible Pump. A pump placed down the well to push oil to the surface.
Hydrogen Sulfide. A deadly, poisonous gas often found in oil wells (rotten egg smell).
Health, Safety, and Environment. The department/rules focused on safety.
Drilling Fluid. The special liquid pumped down the hole to cool the bit and carry cuttings.
Personal Protective Equipment. Hard hats, safety glasses, FR clothing, boots.
The machine used to drill or work over a well.
Rate of Penetration. How fast the drill bit is drilling (feet per hour).
True Vertical Depth. The vertical distance from surface to the bottom (straight down).
Estimated Ultimate Recovery. The total amount of oil/gas a well is expected to produce in its entire life.
Gas-Oil Ratio. The volume of gas produced per barrel of oil. High GOR can indicate reservoir pressure changes.
Lease Operating Expense. The cost to run the well (electricity, chemicals, labor). If LOE > Revenue, the well is shut in.
Pressure Safety Valve. A mechanical valve set to pop open at a specific pressure to prevent a vessel from exploding.
Reid Vapor Pressure. A measure of how volatile the oil is. Pipelines have strict RVP limits (oil cannot be too "gassy").
Vapor Recovery Unit. A compressor that captures low-pressure gas from tanks to sell it, rather than venting/flaring it.
Authorization for Expenditure. The budget document proposing costs for a specific project (like drilling a well).
Barrel. The standard unit of volume for oil. Equal to 42 U.S. gallons.
Bottom Hole Assembly. The collection of tools at the bottom of the drill string (bit, motor, sensors).
Bottom Hole Pressure. The pressure measured at the bottom of the well.
The tool at the end of the drill string that cuts through the rock.
Blowout Preventer. A massive valve stack on the wellhead used to seal the well in an emergency.
Barrels of Oil Equivalent. A way to combine oil and gas volumes into one number for reporting.

Electric Submersible Pump. A long, skinny electric motor and pump stack usually placed at the bottom of the well. It pushes fluid up rather than pulling it.
Progressing Cavity Pump. A screw-type pump. A spiral metal rotor spins inside a rubber stator, squeezing fluid up like a screw conveyor. Good for thick/sandy oil.
Lease Operating Expense. The total monthly bill to run the field.
Total Depth. The final depth the well reaches.
